newsitem.title: JAPAN: Yen fall causes lifestyle adjustments in Japan.
newsitem.headline: Yen fall causes lifestyle adjustments in Japan.

text.p: Psst, got any dollars you want to sell?

While it hasn't quite reached that stage on the back streets of Tokyo, the 50 percent fall in the yen's value in the past two years is causing some lifestyle adjustments for Japanese consumers used to snapping up luxury foreign goods and jetting around the world.
Couples on a date are a little more careful in ordering the wine, the trip to Paris is not as long as it was, or maybe not even possible, and brand-name luggage is no longer a necessity.
Sending children abroad to study is a harder decision and landlords are finding more foreigners competing for the capital's choicest appartments.
No one suggests Japan is becoming a deprived nation. Far from it.
Tokyo's restaurants are still full, new luxury super-malls are opening and residents are still among the world's best dressed.
But life in general has become a more frugal affair.
Overseas tourism, for foreigners once the most visible symbol of Japan's economic might, is gradually slowing down.

"Up to last April, the number of people travelling abroad had steadily shown a double digit increase each month. But since last May the rate of increase has dropped to one digit, mainly because of a weakening yen," said a spokesman for Japan Travel Bureau (JTB), the country's biggest travel agent.
"The recent drop in the yen is not a bright factor for us. We may have to raise prices again," he said.
Last year JTB first raised prices of package tours by 3.4 percent and then increased them by a further 2.4 percent.
Japan's National Tourist Organisation (JNTO) agrees.
"We don't make any predictions but we certainly feel a weak yen is going to have a bigger and bigger negative effect on the outflow of Japanese tourists," a JNTO official said.
Luggage-maker Louis Vuitton Japan KK, like many foreign sellers of luxury products, plans to raise prices by an average 4.5 percent from February to cope with the weak yen.
"I can't tell what effect the increases are going to have on sales," a spokeswoman said.
Not everyone is unhappy.
A journalist for a U.S. newspaper who is paid in dollars said he counts himself among the winners from the yen's decline.
"When I came to Japan three years ago, my budget was based on 110 yen to the dollar. Then it dropped to 80 yen," he said.
"With my rent going up and my salary dropping more than 20 percent, I started to look for another job. But now, at 120 yen to the dollar, the financial pressure has disappeared."
Ken Corp, a Tokyo real estate firm specialising in apartments for foreigners, sees a similar trend.

"The number of foreigners renting apartments through us has been increasing since late last year," a company spokeswoman said. "We believe that's because of the foreign exchange rates and a possible increase in the budgets of their companies."
Kawachiya Shuhan Co, Japan's biggest discount liquor store chain, which sells almost all kinds of foreign brandy, whiskey, wine and beer, is not cheering.
"We have been hard-hit by the weakening yen. For example, we had to raise prices of French wine by 10 percent at the start of the New Year," company president Yukio Higuchi said.
"With the yen weakening to 120 or more to the dollar, we will have to raise prices again soon," he said.
Education Ministry officials, who advise Japanese on sending children abroad to study, sense the number may be dropping.
"We are still not in a position to assess the impact of the weak yen on people wanting to study abroad," one official said.
"But it is common sense that if the yen continues to weaken, the number of people who are willing and can afford to go abroad to study is likely to drop," he added.
